column4: Identify and record every AI system, model, tool, agent and use case in the organisation, including embedded vendor AI and shadow use.
column5: AI register with owner, purpose, data used, vendor, risk tier and lifecycle status for each entry; date of last review.
column6: Pick three business units at random. Does every AI tool they use appear in the register?
column7: Chief AI Officer / AI governance lead

column4: Apply one consistent method to rate AI risk by impact and likelihood, and tie each tier to the controls and approvals it requires.
column5: Approved risk methodology; risk tier recorded against every register entry; documented tier-to-control matrix.
column6: Can two assessors rate the same use case independently and land on the same tier?

column4: Stand up a cross-functional AI governance body with clear terms of reference, decision rights and a named accountable owner for every AI system.
column5: Terms of reference; membership spanning risk, legal, privacy, security, data and business; minutes showing decisions made.
column6: For any production AI system, can you name the one person accountable for it in under a minute?

column4: Approve and publish policies covering ethics, acceptable use, data, model governance and accountability, and train people on them.
column5: Board- or executive-approved AI policy; review date; staff attestation or training completion records.
column6: Ask five staff where the AI policy lives and what it forbids. How many can answer?

column4: Use standard templates such as model cards and datasheets so every system can be understood, audited and handed over.
column5: Completed model card and data sheet per system, version-controlled, covering intended use, limits, training data provenance and evaluation results.
column6: Could an auditor who has never seen the system reconstruct what it does and why from the documentation alone?

column4: Test models for bias across relevant groups, disaggregated rather than in aggregate, and act on what you find.
column5: Fairness test plan with defined groups and thresholds; disaggregated results; remediation log for findings.
column6: Are results reported per group, and is there a written threshold that would block release?

column4: Set the level of explanation each system must provide based on the risk and impact of its decisions, including to affected people.
column5: Explainability standard by risk tier; sample explanations; human review and challenge route for affected individuals.
column6: If a person asks why the system decided against them, what exactly do you send them, and who sends it?
column10: Art. 13, 14, 86 (transparency, human oversight, right to explanation)

column4: Protect data, models and outputs with security and privacy safeguards, including AI-specific threats such as prompt injection and data leakage.
column5: Privacy impact assessment; AI threat model; red-team or penetration test results; access controls on training data and prompts.
column6: Has the system been attacked on purpose (prompt injection, data exfiltration) before go-live, and were the findings fixed?

column4: Monitor performance, data drift, fairness and system behaviour in production, with alerts that reach a named person.
column5: Monitoring dashboard; defined metrics and thresholds; alert routing; drift and performance reports over time.
column6: If accuracy dropped 10% after a vendor model update, who would get the alert, and how fast?

column4: Define how AI incidents are detected, escalated, contained, remediated and reported, and rehearse it.
column5: AI incident playbook; severity definitions; incident log; at least one tabletop exercise with lessons learned.
column6: Can you switch the system off or roll it back today, and has anyone practised doing it?

column4: Track changing laws and standards and run periodic compliance assessments and independent audits.
column5: Regulatory horizon register; compliance assessment schedule; internal audit reports and management responses.
column6: When did a law affecting your AI last change, and how long did it take you to notice?

column4: Set clear rules for safe, responsible and compliant use of generative AI tools and models, including approved tools and data limits.
column5: Generative AI standard; approved-tools list; data classification rules for prompts; output review and labelling requirements.
column6: Do staff know which tools are approved, and what data they must never paste into them?
